question: On flexible nasopharyngolaryngoscopy, a 60-year-old smoker is found to have an exophytic lesion confined to one true vocal cord with normal cord mobility. Which of the following statements about this presentation is most accurate?

answers.text: This is likely a supraglottic carcinoma, which typically presents with hoarseness as the earliest symptom.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Supraglottic carcinomas do NOT typically cause early hoarseness because the true cords are not primarily involved; patients often present late with dysphagia, neck mass, or referred otalgia. Early hoarseness points to glottic origin.

answers.text: This is consistent with a glottic carcinoma; early hoarseness is characteristic because even a small cord lesion disrupts phonation.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Glottic (true cord) carcinomas cause hoarseness very early because the vocal cords are the phonatory organ. This early symptom and the sparse lymphatic supply of the glottis mean T1 glottic carcinomas carry an excellent prognosis with radiotherapy or laser cordectomy.

answers.text: Normal cord mobility excludes malignancy; a biopsy is not indicated.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Normal cord mobility simply indicates that the lesion has not yet invaded the paraglottic space or cricoarytenoid joint. An exophytic lesion on the cord in a smoker mandates biopsy regardless of mobility status.

answers.text: A subglottic lesion is the most likely diagnosis given the anatomical site described.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The description is of a lesion on the true vocal cord — this is the glottis by definition. Subglottic lesions are located below the true cords and would not be described as 'on the vocal cord'.

overallFeedback.feedback: Key distinction: glottic carcinoma causes early hoarseness (true cord involved), has sparse lymphatics, and has a good prognosis when detected early. Supraglottic carcinoma is silent until late, presents with dysphagia or neck nodes, and has a worse prognosis due to rich lymphatic drainage.
Correct. Glottic carcinoma presents early with hoarseness; supraglottic carcinoma presents late. This distinction is a core EN clinical knowledge point with direct management implications.
